meta.about: Generated quiz decks on the Quiz page (assets/js/view-quiz.js): "Which Concept?" matches an own-words cue to one of the Twelve Concepts; "Which committee does this?" matches a duty to a Conference committee (FCR.COMMITTEES id) or a trustees' committee (FCR.TRUSTEES_COMMITTEES key, or a key in trustees_extra).
meta.source: The A.A. Service Manual 2026-2028 (BM-31): Twelve Concepts short and long forms and essays (pp. C-IV to C-59); Conference committees pp. 46-48; General Service Board committees pp. 58-60. Printed page numbers.
meta.rules: Own words, page-cited. A cue never contains its Concept's number or title words; a duty never names its committee and starts with a verb (the question reads "Which ... committee <duty>?"). "also": answers that fit too, never offered as wrong options. "bank": the duty repeats a learn.json bank question, so the merged All and Service Manual decks skip it.

concept_cues.cue: The last word on A.A.'s world services always rests with the group conscience of the whole Fellowship.
News in 1948 of Dr. Bob's fatal illness showed that the co-founders were almost the only link between the groups and a little-known board.
The first Conference, in 1951, was a test of whether Tradition Two could work for A.A. as a whole, trustees and founders included.
Bill W. contrasts A.A. with nations whose group conscience is giving way to apathy and power-seeking, and trusts A.A.'s democracy of service to hold.
For nearly every practical purpose, the Conference speaks and acts as the whole Society's conscience in its world affairs.
Scattered groups cannot run world services themselves, so they entrust operating power to chosen servants who can speak and act for them.
The groups gave the Conference full charge of world services, except for changing the Traditions or the Charter's General Warranties.
In 1937 the Akron and New York groups first entrusted Dr. Bob and Bill W. with creating services to carry the message worldwide.
Step by step, the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation took over money matters, the book, public relations and then the Grapevine.
Each service body may choose which matters to settle on its own and which to report, consult on, or send up for direction.
Delegates are world servants of A.A. first and area representatives second, so on a final vote they follow their own judgment and conscience.
An 'instructed' delegate who cannot vote their own conscience on a final vote is no trusted servant, only a messenger.
This latitude must never become an excuse for skipping reports, overstepping defined limits or failing to consult those entitled to be consulted.
It rests on mutual trust: we trust God, A.A. and each other, so we trust our leaders in service as well.
Each class of world servants should get a vote in reasonable proportion to the responsibility it carries.
This is why trustees, the AAWS and Grapevine directors and their staffs are voting members of the Conference.
Paid staff cannot become trustees, but they are invited to board meetings and may join the debate without a vote.
A trustee-treasurer once tore up the office paychecks; no one of us should hold absolute power over money and people.
Just as there are no second-class A.A.s, there should be no second-class world service workers.
Minorities in staffs, committees and boards are urged to file minority reports when they believe a majority is seriously wrong.
Any worker, paid or unpaid, may take a personal grievance straight to the General Service Board without fear of reprisal.
A minority that is fully heard is the best guard against a majority that is misinformed, hasty or angry.
Bill W. cites de Tocqueville's warning that democracy's greatest danger is the tyranny of apathetic, self-seeking or angry majorities.
The Conference keeps the final word on large matters of policy and finance, but in most of them the General Service Board takes the lead and does the active work.
In Bill W.'s business picture, the groups are the stockholders, the delegates their proxies, and the board a holding company.
The General Service Board acts as A.A.'s banker, the active guardian of its Traditions and the steward of its worldwide public relations.
So the board can act freely when the Conference is not meeting, the Conference grants it wide administrative latitude.
The board's Charter and Bylaws hold up in court; the Conference Charter does not, and relies on custom and the A.A. purse.
In a showdown the delegates could cut off the groups' money, so the Conference's practical power nearly always outweighs the board's.
Like a U.S. President who seldom vetoes a bill, the trustees hold a veto over Conference actions but rarely use it.
The trustees may cut a Conference-approved budget during the year, but should not substantially exceed it without consulting.
The board itself handles the large questions of policy and finance, but not the day-to-day running of AAWS and the Grapevine.
The General Service Board oversees the active service corporations mainly through its power to elect all of their directors.
Each service corporation should have its own charter, working capital, executive, employees, offices and equipment.
The board must never become an operating company: its chair, usually nonalcoholic and unpaid, cannot be a full-time executive.
Keep money and executive power spread out; never concentrate them in a single service entity.
The founders' former role at the head of A.A.'s world affairs must pass to the board of trustees.
Groups should choose GSRs with care, since only GSRs name the committee members and, finally, the delegates.
A 'politico' tries to give people what they want; a statesman knows when not to.
Vision, the ability to estimate the future soundly, is the very essence of prudence.
Opposition for its own sake never works; when asked, always give your reasons, and sound ones.
Every service job should come with matching power to do it, its scope set by custom, resolution, job description or charter.
Double-headed business or policy management is to be avoided at all costs.
Where two committees share a question, name a senior jurisdiction, hear the junior one, and make clear where final settlement lies.
Final power to correct or reorganize should almost never be used in full, only when delegated work has gone wrong.
The trustees should always have the ablest standing committees, corporate directors, executives, staff and consultants.
People tend to recommend associates a little less able than themselves, so those who nominate must guard against it.
Paid workers should be paid in reasonable relation to what similar work earns in the business world.
Staff members rotate through the assignments on equal pay, so no single departure can cripple the office.
No committee can run an active service day to day; its executive direction must head up in one person.
The Conference must never become a seat of dangerous wealth or power.
Important matters are settled by discussion, vote and, whenever possible, substantial unanimity.
No Conference action may ever punish a person or stir up public controversy.
Changing this part of the Conference Charter takes the written consent of three-quarters of the listed groups that vote, with six months allowed.
The Conference may serve A.A. but must never perform acts of government, and must stay democratic in thought and action.
Many members call it 'The A.A. Service Bill of Rights'.

committee_scopes.duty: Reviews and approves the format and content of the week's schedule for the annual Conference.
Weighs proposed themes, workshops and presentation or discussion topics for the Conference, plus its evaluation questionnaire.
Suggests policies and activities that carry the message by sharing information about A.A. with people who deal with alcoholics in their work.
Helps members and outside organizations see how A.A. can work alongside others without affiliating.
Reviews A.A. efforts to bridge the gap for alcoholics leaving jail or prison.
Supports members who carry the message to alcoholics behind the walls.
Reviews every aspect of service to A.A. groups inside jails and prisons.
Recommends needed updates to the material used to carry the message into jails and prisons.
Clarifies what A.A. can and cannot do, within the Traditions, for alcoholics in custody and after release.
Reviews the budgets and the income-and-expense reports of A.A. World Services and AA Grapevine.
Reviews or starts Conference recommendations that involve money.
Keeps abreast of the Fellowship's needs, including yearly budgets and the income that service work requires.
Reviews how the Fellowship's two magazines are developed and circulated, and seeks suggestions on their material and format.
Helps clarify policy questions about A.A.'s international journals.
Reaches Spanish-speaking alcoholics through the Fellowship's bimonthly Spanish-language magazine.
Develops material related to the magazines and considers topics for future books drawn from them.
Focuses on recovery material, leaving service material for a particular field, such as prison work, to that field's committee.
Reviews proposals for new and revised pamphlets and books, and recommends new pamphlets, books or audiovisual items.
Reviews new formats of existing items, including digital and audiovisual ones.
Examines the general principles under which the Conference itself operates.
Decides on requests from other countries' boards and GSOs to attend the annual Conference as observers.
Reviews requests to temporarily replace a delegate who is unable to attend the Conference.
Reviews proposals to change or expand the Conference, such as requests for new delegate areas, and steps that affect its cost.
Builds understanding of A.A., and heads off misunderstanding, through print, broadcast and online media and outreach meetings.
Reviews outreach pamphlets and PSAs.
Reaches out to young people and students about A.A.
Reviews the membership survey data and how the survey is done.
Communicates with people who work in the media, and evaluates digital and social media efforts to carry the message.
Reviews The A.A. Service Manual, discusses suggestions and recommends changes.
Checks each year's draft of the Conference's published record for accuracy.
Reviews and recommends any needed changes to the document that defines the Conference itself.
Supports members and groups who carry the message into rehabilitation facilities.
Reviews A.A. efforts to bridge the gap from rehab to A.A.
Supports efforts to bring the message to people who face barriers to it, including those in underserved or remote communities.
Reviews service to A.A. meetings in rehab and other institutions outside the prison system.
Reviews the résumés of all nominees for the General Service Board and the corporate boards.
Presents the slates of board nominees to the Conference for disapproval, if any.
Is part of the voting body that nominates regional and at-large board members during Conference week.
Considers matters of practice and policy about A.A.'s historical records.
Is a secondary committee on A.A.'s historical records that may take direct action at its dinner meeting.
Has eight delegate members drawn by lot, one from each region.
Considers and develops plans for the coming worldwide A.A. gatherings held every five years.
Offers input on carrying out the regional, special and local sharing sessions that keep the board and GSO staff in touch with members.
Makes sure, with expert guidance from GSO, that A.A.'s historical collection is preserved, organized and used to the highest professional and ethical standards.
Reviews research and access requests for A.A.'s historical collection.
Seeks mutual understanding with people concerned with alcoholism in their work, so A.A. is accepted in hospitals and rehab centers.
Considers resources for alcoholics in rehab and for those who carry the message to them.
Seeks to widen the reach of the message in remote places where language, culture or geography are barriers.
Develops programs and materials that support carrying the message to alcoholics in jails and prisons.
Seeks ways to develop and expand pre-release contacts and services.
Seeks to expand, across the U.S. and Canada, the service that lets incarcerated alcoholics write to A.A. members on the outside.
Oversees all AAWS and Grapevine money matters, the General Fund, the Reserve Fund and the Postretirement Medical Fund.
Is chaired by the treasurer of the General Service Board.
Works on the procedures, agenda and theme of the annual meeting of delegates, trustees, directors and staff.
Considers how the workload is spread among the delegates' committees.
Considers innovations for better communication among the members of the annual meeting.
Suggests ways to carry the message to alcoholics abroad, especially in countries with no service structure yet.
Shares experience, supports translating A.A. literature into other languages and encourages wider regional or zonal meetings.
Is the main link between A.A. in other countries and the U.S./Canada General Service Board.
Plans the worldwide gatherings held every five years and all the regional, local and special sharing sessions.
Assesses how well the worldwide gatherings and sharing sessions work, and suggests changes to serve the Fellowship better.
Responds to requests to explore new items, and reviews existing ones for revision or discontinuance.
Develops new and revised Conference-approved pamphlets and books.
Oversees the yearly updates to The A.A. Service Manual recommended by the Conference.
Reviews the procedures for selecting candidates.
Reviews for approval all nontrustee director candidates of AAWS and AA Grapevine, and the general service trustees put forward by the two corporate boards.
Takes part in the Conference sessions that select regional trustees and trustees-at-large.
Oversees the development of the board's policies and projects for telling the world about A.A.
Carries out pending Conference Advisory Actions on media outreach.
Builds wider understanding of A.A. through the media, outreach meetings, talks to civic groups, films and broadcast announcements.
Meets at least once a year with the independent accountants who examine the books of the GSB, AAWS and AA Grapevine, to discuss internal controls.
Recommends each year which independent accounting firm the board should engage.
Meets yearly with outside consultants to check that the affiliates' pay practices, including executive pay, are appropriate.
Covers pay philosophy and the yearly salary-increase process, though the affiliates' own boards make the actual pay decisions.
Reviews and upholds the processes in the board's Code of Conduct and Confidentiality Policy.
Is made up of five randomly selected returning trustees, including an alternate, supported by the GSO staff coordinator.
Administers the staff pension plan and sets its investment policy with the board's investment advisors.
